1. Introduction to Macroeconomics

Learning goals

Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: income, employment, inflation, unemployment and deficits. It works in four steps: document the facts, build a model, compare the model with the facts, and use the model for experiments. By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

  • describe the big facts behind the questions of macroeconomics, using real data for many countries;
  • explain the structure of an economic model: parameters and exogenous variables go in, and endogenous variables come out;
  • derive the equilibrium wage and employment of the supply-and-demand model of the labor market, read the comparative statics of each parameter, and derive the unemployment a minimum wage creates;
  • derive the compound-growth formula, the average annual growth rate and the rule of 70, and explain why steady growth draws a straight line on a ratio scale;
  • derive the link between the employment-population ratio and the unemployment rate, and measure the output gap;
  • tell the long run (economic growth) from the short run (fluctuations around potential output);
  • load data tables with pandas, check them, and draw interactive line charts with Plotly;
  • write short Python functions and turn them into interactive figures with sliders.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each model figure gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

The data figures of this chapter let you add other countries. On the website, a menu above each of these figures adds a group of countries (the G7, a world region, …); the next cell builds those menus.

Show the helper code 
# @title Helpers for the website's country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def country_traces(data, y, skip, x="year", fmt=".1f", markers=False):
    """One line per country of a long table (country, x, y), leaving out the countries in skip."""
    extra = {}
    for name, part in data.groupby("country"):
        if name not in skip:
            extra[name] = [go.Scatter(x=part[x], y=part[y], name=name, mode="lines+markers" if markers else "lines",
                                      line=dict(color=COLORS[name], width=2),
                                      hovertemplate=f"<b>{name}</b><br>%{{x}}: %{{y:{fmt}}}<extra></extra>")]
    return extra


def country_menu(fig, extra, countries):
    """Add the extra countries' traces hidden, and a menu that shows one group of them (G7, a region, ...).

    The traces already in fig (the textbook's) stay as they are, and slider steps only switch those."""
    n = len(fig.data)
    owner = []
    for name, traces in extra.items():
        for trace in traces:
            trace.visible = False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(name)
    groups = {"G7": countries.country[countries.g7], "G20": countries.country[countries.g20],
              "OECD": countries.country[countries.oecd]}
    for region in sorted(countries.region.unique()):
        groups[region] = countries.country[countries.region == region]
    rest, autoscale = list(range(n, len(fig.data))), {"yaxis.autorange": True}
    buttons = [dict(label="Textbook only", method="update", args=[{"visible": [False] * len(owner)}, autoscale, rest])]
    for label, members in groups.items():
        visible = [o in set(members) for o in owner]
        if any(visible):
            buttons.append(dict(label=f"+ {label} ({sum(visible)})", method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, autoscale, rest]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=0, x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    for slider in fig.layout.sliders:
        for step in slider.steps:
            step.args = [{"visible": list(step.args[0]["visible"])}, step.args[1], list(range(n))]
    return fig
Show the helper code 
# @title Helper for the website's one-country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def dropdown_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Like slider_figure, but with a dropdown menu: one precomputed figure per value (e.g. per country)."""
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[values.index(start)].layout)
    owner = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (values[i] == start)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(), "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes], "yaxis": f.layout.yaxis.to_plotly_json(),
                  "xaxis": f.layout.xaxis.to_plotly_json()}
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": [o == i for o in owner]}, layout]))
    menu = dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=values.index(start), x=1, xanchor="right", y=1.02, yanchor="bottom")
    fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[menu], margin=dict(t=110))
    return fig

Model overview

Macroeconomics asks big questions: why living standards in some countries are many times those in others, why whole economies sometimes shrink, and why prices sometimes rise quickly. To answer them, economists first collect the facts and then build a model: a simplified economy written as a few equations. We feed the model some numbers that we choose, and it tells us the outcomes we want to explain.

This first chapter has no large model yet, but it already relies on four tools that return in every later chapter, and this section derives each of them step by step. The first two are measurement tools: the rates and ratios behind the facts of Figs. 1–5, and the arithmetic of compound growth behind Figs. 1 and 7. The last two show how a model works, with the smallest model there is: supply and demand in the labor market, first on its own and then with a minimum wage (Figs. 6 and 8). At the end, ### The model in code turns the results into Python functions and checks each of them with numbers.

A bar over a letter marks a parameter, a number the model builder chooses, such as \(\bar{a}\) or \(\bar{f}\). Letters without a bar are endogenous variables: the model determines them. A subscript \(t\) marks the year, as in \(y_t\). In the code we simply write a, l and f.

Measuring the facts: rates, ratios and the output gap

Definitions

Almost every number in this chapter is a rate or a ratio, not a total. Dividing by the right total makes a small country comparable with a large one, and 1960 comparable with 2025.

  • Inflation. Let \(P_t\) be the price level in year \(t\), for example a consumer price index. The inflation rate is the percentage change of prices over one year (Fig. 3): \[\pi_t = 100\times\frac{P_t - P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}.\]
  • Jobs. Each adult is employed (\(E\)), unemployed (\(U\): has no job but is looking for one), or out of the labor force. The labor force is \(LF = E + U\), and \(Pop\) is the adult population. Three ratios describe the labor market: \[u = \frac{U}{LF}\ \ \text{(unemployment rate, Fig. 4)}, \qquad e = \frac{E}{Pop}\ \ \text{(employment-population ratio, Fig. 2)}, \qquad p = \frac{LF}{Pop}\ \ \text{(participation rate)}.\]
  • Deficits. With \(Y\) for GDP, both deficits of Fig. 5 are measured as shares of GDP: \[\text{budget deficit} = \frac{\text{government spending} - \text{government revenue}}{Y}, \qquad \text{trade deficit} = \frac{\text{imports} - \text{exports}}{Y}.\] A negative deficit is a surplus.
  • Potential output. \(Y^{pot}_t\) is what the economy would produce if all prices could adjust freely and all workers and machines were fully used. Actual output \(Y_t\) moves around it (Fig. 7).

Deriving the key relations

Step 1: from inflation back to prices. Multiply the definition of \(\pi_t\) by \(P_{t-1}/100\), then add \(P_{t-1}\) to both sides:

\[P_t = P_{t-1}\left(1 + \frac{\pi_t}{100}\right).\]

Each year multiplies the price level by a factor \(1 + \pi_t/100\). Inflation of 3,080 percent, as in Argentina in 1989 (Fig. 3), multiplies prices by \(1 + 30.8 = 31.8\) in a single year. For prices to rise a thousandfold within one year we need \(1 + \pi/100 = 1000\), that is \(\pi = 99{,}900\) percent. Over several years the yearly factors multiply:

\[\frac{P_T}{P_0} = \left(1 + \frac{\pi_1}{100}\right)\left(1 + \frac{\pi_2}{100}\right)\cdots\left(1 + \frac{\pi_T}{100}\right).\]

Two years of 10 percent inflation raise prices by \(1.1 \times 1.1 = 1.21\), that is by 21 percent and not 20: the second year’s inflation also applies to the first year’s increase.

Step 2: employment, participation and unemployment. Start from \(E = LF - U\) and divide both sides by \(Pop\). Then take \(LF/Pop\) out as a common factor:

\[e = \frac{E}{Pop} = \frac{LF - U}{Pop} = \frac{LF}{Pop}\left(1 - \frac{U}{LF}\right),\]

so that

\[e = p\,(1 - u). \tag{1}\]

The share of adults with a job is the share in the labor force times the share of the labor force that has a job. So the employment-population ratio of Fig. 2 can fall for two different reasons: more people are unemployed, or people stop looking for work. In February 2020 about 63.3 percent of U.S. adults were in the labor force and 3.5 percent of them were unemployed, so \(e = 63.3 \times (1 - 0.035) \approx 61.1\) percent, the value in Fig. 2.

Step 3: the output gap. The gap measures how far actual output is from potential, in percent of potential:

\[\text{gap}_t = 100\times\left(\frac{Y_t}{Y^{pot}_t} - 1\right). \tag{2}\]

Multiplying out gives the gap in dollars, \(Y_t - Y^{pot}_t = (\text{gap}_t/100)\times Y^{pot}_t\). The same formula works per person: dividing both outputs by the population leaves the ratio \(Y_t/Y^{pot}_t\) unchanged, so the gap in percent is the same, and the gap in dollars per person is \((\text{gap}_t/100)\times Y^{pot}_t/Pop_t\). For small gaps, \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) (Appendix C.6) gives the log form \(\text{gap}_t \approx 100\,(\ln Y_t - \ln Y^{pot}_t)\). The short-run chapters measure fluctuations in this way.

Step 4: why divide by GDP. The growth rate of a ratio is the growth rate of its numerator minus that of its denominator (Appendix C.5). For a deficit \(D\),

\[g_{D/Y} \approx g_D - g_Y.\]

A deficit that grows as fast as GDP keeps the same weight in the economy, even though in dollars it is many times larger than in 1960. That is why Fig. 5 compares shares of GDP and not dollars.

What the numbers tell us

The two labor-market ratios. The table reads equation (1) one input at a time, at the February 2020 values \(p = 63.3\%\) and \(u = 3.5\%\):

A change of … changes \(e = p(1-u)\) by Why
\(+1\) point in the unemployment rate \(u\) \(-p \approx -0.63\) points a point of \(u\) is a point of the labor force, not of all adults
\(+1\) point in the participation rate \(p\) \(+(1-u) \approx +0.97\) points most new participants find a job

In logs, \(\ln e = \ln p + \ln(1-u)\) (Appendix C.4), so the percentage change of \(e\) splits exactly into a participation part and an unemployment part. By April 2020 participation had dropped to about 60.1 percent and unemployment had jumped to about 14.8 percent. The check in ### The model in code shows that roughly 70 percent of the fall in \(e\) came from higher unemployment and 30 percent from people leaving the labor force.

The output gap is negative in a recession and positive in a boom. Its log form is accurate only for small gaps: for a gap as deep as the Great Depression’s, the two versions differ by about 2 points (see the check below).

Growth rates and compound growth

Definitions

The growth rate of a variable \(y_t\), such as GDP per person, from year \(t\) to year \(t+1\) is its percentage change, written as a decimal:

\[g_t = \frac{y_{t+1} - y_t}{y_t} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad y_{t+1} = y_t\,(1 + g_t).\]

The inflation rate of the block above is the growth rate of the price level, times 100. The average annual growth rate between year 0 and year \(T\) is the one constant rate \(g\) that would carry \(y_0\) to \(y_T\) in \(T\) years.

Solving: compound growth

Step 1: growth at a constant rate. If \(y\) grows at the same rate \(g\) every year, apply the rule year after year and substitute each line into the next:

\[y_1 = y_0(1+g), \qquad y_2 = y_1(1+g) = y_0(1+g)^2, \qquad y_3 = y_2(1+g) = y_0(1+g)^3, \qquad \dots\]

After \(t\) years, therefore,

\[y_t = y_0\,(1+g)^t. \tag{3}\]

This is compound growth (Appendix C.3): each year’s growth applies to a level that already includes the growth of all the years before.

Step 2: the average growth rate. Solve equation (3) for \(g\), with \(T\) years. Divide by \(y_0\), raise both sides to the power \(1/T\) (because \(\left((1+g)^T\right)^{1/T} = 1+g\)), and subtract 1:

\[\frac{y_T}{y_0} = (1+g)^T \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left(\frac{y_T}{y_0}\right)^{1/T} = 1 + g \quad\Longrightarrow\quad g = \left(\frac{y_T}{y_0}\right)^{1/T} - 1. \tag{4}\]

Fig. 7 applies this formula to U.S. GDP per person from 1870 to 2025, with \(T = 155\): the answer is about 1.9 percent a year. Read backwards, the same formula tells us the growth rate a target needs: a tenfold rise in a century needs \(g = 10^{1/100} - 1 \approx 2.3\) percent a year.

Step 3: logs and the ratio scale. Take the natural log of equation (3), using \(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\) and \(\ln(x^t) = t\ln x\) (Appendix C.4):

\[\ln y_t = \ln y_0 + t\,\ln(1+g).\]

The log of \(y\) is a straight line in time, with slope \(\ln(1+g)\). A ratio scale draws exactly this, so a series that grows at a constant rate is a straight line in Figs. 1 and 7, and a steeper line means faster growth. Every doubling covers the same vertical distance, because \(\ln(2y) - \ln y = \ln 2\) whatever the level of \(y\). For small \(g\), \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\) (Appendix C.6), which gives a second way to compute an average growth rate: \(g \approx (\ln y_T - \ln y_0)/T\).

Step 4: the rule of 70. How many years does it take for \(y\) to double? Put \(y_T/y_0 = 2\) into equation (3) and take logs: \(T\ln(1+g) = \ln 2\), so \(T = \ln 2/\ln(1+g)\). Now use \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\) and \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\):

\[T_{\text{double}} \approx \frac{0.70}{g} = \frac{70}{100\,g}. \tag{5}\]

In words: divide 70 by the growth rate in percent. At 1.9 percent a year, U.S. income per person doubles about every \(70/1.9 \approx 37\) years, a little over four doublings between 1870 and 2025.

What the model predicts

Small differences in growth rates add up. Write equation (3) for two countries and divide one by the other. Relative income changes by the factor \(\left((1+g_1)/(1+g_2)\right)^t\), and in logs

\[\ln\frac{y_{1,t}}{y_{2,t}} = \ln\frac{y_{1,0}}{y_{2,0}} + t\left[\ln(1+g_1) - \ln(1+g_2)\right] \approx \ln\frac{y_{1,0}}{y_{2,0}} + t\,(g_1 - g_2).\]

A gap of only half a percentage point, kept up for 150 years, changes relative income by \(0.005 \times 150 = 0.75\) in logs, a factor of \(e^{0.75} \approx 2.1\). That is about what happened between the United States and Argentina (Fig. 7).

How the growth rate moves the outcomes. The log form gives the effect of the growth rate on the level after \(T\) years: \(d\ln y_T/dg = T/(1+g) \approx T\). One extra point of growth for 100 years adds about \(100 \times 0.01 = 1\) to \(\ln y_{100}\), which multiplies the final level by about \(e \approx 2.7\). The table shows the same effect exactly, from equations (3) and (5):

Growth rate \(g\) Exact doubling time \(\ln 2/\ln(1+g)\) Rule of 70 Factor after 100 years, \((1+g)^{100}\)
1% 69.7 years 70 years 2.7
2% 35.0 years 35 years 7.2
3% 23.4 years 23.3 years 19.2
5% 14.2 years 14 years 131.5

The rule of 70 is very close for the growth rates of rich countries, and it only begins to drift for fast growth such as 10 percent a year.

How a model works: the labor market

Assumptions

Every model in this book has the same structure. The model builder chooses the inputs, and the model’s equations determine the outcomes:

  • parameters are inputs that stay fixed, unless the model builder changes them in an experiment;
  • exogenous variables are inputs that may change over time, along a path the model builder sets in advance (for example a population that grows by 1 percent a year);
  • endogenous variables are the outcomes, the unknowns that the equations solve for.

The smallest example is a single market for hours of work, with a single wage \(w\). Three equations describe it:

\[L^s = \bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} \quad\text{(labor supply)}, \qquad L^d = \bar{f} - w \quad\text{(labor demand)}, \qquad L^s = L^d \quad\text{(the market clears)}.\]

Symbol Role Meaning
\(\bar{a} > 0\) parameter the slope of labor supply: extra hours offered when the wage rises by one dollar
\(\bar{\ell}\) parameter (or an exogenous variable) hours people offer even at a zero wage; it would grow with the population
\(\bar{f}\) parameter hours the firm would hire at a zero wage, a measure of its capacity
\(w\), \(L^s\), \(L^d\) endogenous variables the wage, the hours supplied and the hours demanded

Labor supply slopes up: a higher wage draws out more hours. Labor demand slopes down: each extra dollar of wage makes one hour less worth hiring. The model has three equations and three unknowns. Once the market clears, \(L^s\) and \(L^d\) are the same number, employment \(L\), so the outcomes are just \(w\) and \(L\). We assume \(\bar{f} > \bar{\ell}\): otherwise workers would offer more hours at a zero wage than the firm wants, and the wage could not be positive.

Solving the model

Step 1: one equation in one unknown. Put the supply and demand equations into the market-clearing condition. Only the wage is left:

\[\bar{a}\,w + \bar{\ell} = \bar{f} - w.\]

Step 2: solve for the wage. Add \(w\) to both sides and subtract \(\bar{\ell}\), so that all the terms with \(w\) are on the left: \(\bar{a}w + w = \bar{f} - \bar{\ell}\), or \((1+\bar{a})\,w = \bar{f} - \bar{\ell}\). Dividing by \(1+\bar{a}\):

\[w^* = \frac{\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}}. \tag{6}\]

Step 3: solve for employment. Put \(w^*\) into the demand equation and write everything over the common denominator \(1+\bar{a}\):

\[L^* = \bar{f} - w^* = \frac{(1+\bar{a})\bar{f} - (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell})}{1+\bar{a}},\]

so that

\[L^* = \frac{\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell}}{1 + \bar{a}}. \tag{7}\]

The supply equation gives the same answer: \(\bar{a}w^* + \bar{\ell} = \left(\bar{a}\bar{f} - \bar{a}\bar{\ell} + \bar{\ell} + \bar{a}\bar{\ell}\right)/(1+\bar{a}) = (\bar{a}\bar{f} + \bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})\). At \(w^*\) the hours offered equal the hours wanted.

Intuition. The wage is high when firms want many hours (\(\bar{f}\) large) compared with the hours people offer anyway (\(\bar{\ell}\) small). Employment is a weighted average of the two, \(L^* = \frac{\bar{a}}{1+\bar{a}}\bar{f} + \frac{1}{1+\bar{a}}\bar{\ell}\): the more strongly workers respond to the wage, the closer employment gets to what firms would like to hire.

Every slider of Figs. 6 and 8 starts from the values of the textbook’s worked exercise, \(\bar{a} = 2\), \(\bar{\ell} = 30\) and \(\bar{f} = 60\). Then \(w^* = (60 - 30)/3 = 10\) and \(L^* = (2\times60 + 30)/3 = 50\).

What the model predicts

The fourth step of the method is to run experiments: change one input and compare the new outcomes with the old ones. Equations (6) and (7) are straight lines in \(\bar{f}\) and \(\bar{\ell}\), so their coefficients are the effects. For \(\bar{a}\) we differentiate (Appendix C.7): \(w^* = (\bar{f}-\bar{\ell})(1+\bar{a})^{-1}\) gives \(dw^*/d\bar{a} = -(\bar{f}-\bar{\ell})/(1+\bar{a})^2 = -w^*/(1+\bar{a})\), and \(L^* = \bar{f} - w^*\) moves by the same amount in the opposite direction.

A rise of 1 in … changes \(w^*\) by changes \(L^*\) by at the baseline Which curve moves
\(\bar{f}\) \(+\dfrac{1}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(+\dfrac{\bar{a}}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(+1/3\) and \(+2/3\) demand shifts right
\(\bar{\ell}\) \(-\dfrac{1}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(+\dfrac{1}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(-1/3\) and \(+1/3\) supply shifts right
\(\bar{a}\) \(-\dfrac{w^*}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(+\dfrac{w^*}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(-3.33\) and \(+3.33\) supply pivots around its zero-wage point

Intuition. A shift of demand is shared between the wage and employment. The wage takes the share \(1/(1+\bar{a})\) and employment the rest: the more responsive workers are, the more a rise in demand shows up as extra hours and the less as higher pay. A shift of supply moves the wage and employment in opposite directions.

Elasticities. Taking logs of equations (6) and (7), \(\ln w^* = \ln(\bar{f}-\bar{\ell}) - \ln(1+\bar{a})\) and \(\ln L^* = \ln(\bar{a}\bar{f}+\bar{\ell}) - \ln(1+\bar{a})\), gives the percentage effects:

A 1% rise in … changes \(w^*\) by changes \(L^*\) by at the baseline
\(\bar{f}\) \(\dfrac{\bar{f}}{\bar{f}-\bar{\ell}}\) \(\dfrac{\bar{a}\bar{f}}{\bar{a}\bar{f}+\bar{\ell}}\) \(+2\%\) and \(+0.8\%\)
\(\bar{\ell}\) \(-\dfrac{\bar{\ell}}{\bar{f}-\bar{\ell}}\) \(\dfrac{\bar{\ell}}{\bar{a}\bar{f}+\bar{\ell}}\) \(-1\%\) and \(+0.2\%\)
\(\bar{a}\) \(-\dfrac{\bar{a}}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(\dfrac{\bar{a}\bar{f}}{\bar{a}\bar{f}+\bar{\ell}} - \dfrac{\bar{a}}{1+\bar{a}}\) \(-0.67\%\) and \(+0.13\%\)

Because the model is made of straight lines rather than powers, these elasticities change with the starting point. The model is far simpler than any real labor market, with one wage and no schooling, training or distance, but it already shows the logic of every later model: write the equations, solve them for the endogenous variables, and read off how each input moves each outcome.

Extension: a minimum wage

Assumptions

The textbook’s example of a parameter is a minimum wage set by law, \(\bar{w}_{\min}\). Keep the three equations above, but forbid any wage below the floor. When the floor is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the floor, and nobody can make the firm hire more hours than it wants at that wage. Employment is then read off the demand curve, and the extra hours that workers offer are unemployment:

\[w = \max(w^*, \bar{w}_{\min}), \qquad L = L^d(w) = \bar{f} - w, \qquad U = L^s(w) - L^d(w).\]

Solving the model

Case 1: the floor does not bind, \(\bar{w}_{\min} \le w^*\). Nothing changes: \(w = w^*\), \(L = L^*\) and \(U = 0\).

Case 2: the floor binds, \(\bar{w}_{\min} > w^*\). Then \(w = \bar{w}_{\min}\). Subtract demand from supply at that wage:

\[U = (\bar{a}\,\bar{w}_{\min} + \bar{\ell}) - (\bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min}) = (1+\bar{a})\,\bar{w}_{\min} - (\bar{f} - \bar{\ell}).\]

Equation (6) says that \(\bar{f} - \bar{\ell} = (1+\bar{a})\,w^*\). Substituting it:

\[U = (1+\bar{a})\,(\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*). \tag{8}\]

Employment is \(L = \bar{f} - \bar{w}_{\min} = L^* - (\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*)\).

Intuition. Each dollar of the floor above \(w^*\) does two things at once: the firm hires one hour less, and workers offer \(\bar{a}\) hours more. The gap between them therefore grows by \(1 + \bar{a}\) hours per dollar. With the baseline values, a floor of 12 is 2 dollars above \(w^* = 10\), so employment falls to \(50 - 2 = 48\) and unemployment is \(3 \times 2 = 6\) hours, the numbers Fig. 6 shows.

What the model predicts

Floor at or below \(w^*\) Floor above \(w^*\)
wage \(w^*\) \(\bar{w}_{\min}\)
employment \(L^*\) \(L^* - (\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*)\)
unemployment \(0\) \((1+\bar{a})(\bar{w}_{\min} - w^*)\)

No curve moves: the floor is a horizontal line in the diagram, and the market slides up the demand curve. Above \(w^*\), each extra dollar of the floor cuts employment by 1 hour and raises unemployment by \(1+\bar{a} = 3\) hours. A floor below the market wage has no effect at all.

The model in code

We now turn the results into Python functions. Each function’s description names the equation it computes. The cells after them check the algebra above with numbers. Every later section of the notebook reuses labor_supply, labor_demand and equilibrium.

Python note. def creates a function: a named recipe that takes inputs (the arguments) and gives back a result with return. Writing a=2.0 gives the argument a default value, used whenever we do not pass one. The text in triple quotes is a short description of what the function does. A function can return two results at once, separated by a comma. ** means “to the power of”, and np.log is the natural logarithm.

def labor_supply(w, a=2.0, l=30.0):
    """Hours of work offered at the wage w: L^s = a w + l."""
    return a * w + l


def labor_demand(w, f=60.0):
    """Hours of work the firm wants to hire at the wage w: L^d = f - w."""
    return f - w


def equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0):
    """The wage and employment at which supply equals demand: equations (6) and (7)."""
    w_star = (f - l) / (1 + a)
    L_star = labor_demand(w_star, f)
    return w_star, L_star


def average_growth(start, end, years):
    """The constant yearly growth rate that turns `start` into `end` in `years` years: equation (4)."""
    return (end / start) ** (1 / years) - 1


def doubling_time(g):
    """Exact number of years it takes to double at the growth rate g: ln 2 / ln(1 + g)."""
    return np.log(2) / np.log(1 + g)

Let us check the functions against the baseline answer. The wage from equation (6), put into either curve, must give the employment of equation (7).

Python note. w_star, L_star = equilibrium() stores the two results of the function in two variables. An f-string such as f"w* = {w_star:.1f}" inserts the value of a variable into a piece of text; :.1f means “show one decimal”.

w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
print(f"Equilibrium wage       w* = {w_star:.1f}")
print(f"Equilibrium employment L* = {L_star:.1f}   (equation 7: {(2 * 60 + 30) / (1 + 2):.1f})")
print(f"At w*, supply = {labor_supply(w_star):.1f} and demand = {labor_demand(w_star):.1f}: the market clears")
Equilibrium wage       w* = 10.0
Equilibrium employment L* = 50.0   (equation 7: 50.0)
At w*, supply = 50.0 and demand = 50.0: the market clears

Check 1: the elasticities. Raise each parameter by 1 percent and see by what percentage \(w^*\) and \(L^*\) change. The table above predicts \(+2\%\) and \(+0.8\%\) for \(\bar{f}\), \(-1\%\) and \(+0.2\%\) for \(\bar{\ell}\), and \(-0.67\%\) and \(+0.13\%\) for \(\bar{a}\).

w0, L0 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0)
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0 * 1.01)
print(f"1% higher f: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0, l=30.0 * 1.01, f=60.0)
print(f"1% higher l: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")
w1, L1 = equilibrium(a=2.0 * 1.01, l=30.0, f=60.0)
print(f"1% higher a: w* {100 * (w1 / w0 - 1):+.2f}%,  L* {100 * (L1 / L0 - 1):+.2f}%")
1% higher f: w* +2.00%,  L* +0.80%
1% higher l: w* -1.00%,  L* +0.20%
1% higher a: w* -0.66%,  L* +0.13%

The answers for \(\bar{f}\) and \(\bar{\ell}\) are exact, because \(w^*\) and \(L^*\) are straight lines in those two parameters. For \(\bar{a}\) they are close but not exact, because an elasticity describes very small changes.

Check 2: the minimum wage. For several floors, we compute unemployment directly, as hours supplied minus hours demanded at the wage that holds, and compare the result with equation (8).

Python note. for w_min in (8, 11, 12, 14): runs the indented lines once for each number in the brackets. max(a, b) is the larger of two numbers, so max(w_star, w_min) is the wage that holds, and max(..., 0) turns a negative formula value into zero when the floor does not bind.

w_star, L_star = equilibrium()
for w_min in (8, 11, 12, 14):
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                                   # the wage that holds
    direct = labor_supply(w) - labor_demand(w)               # hours offered minus hours hired
    formula = max((1 + 2.0) * (w_min - w_star), 0)           # equation (8), zero if the floor does not bind
    print(f"floor {w_min:2d}: wage {w:4.1f}, employment {labor_demand(w):4.1f}, "
          f"unemployment {direct:4.1f} (direct) and {formula:4.1f} (equation 8)")
floor  8: wage 10.0, employment 50.0, unemployment  0.0 (direct) and  0.0 (equation 8)
floor 11: wage 11.0, employment 49.0, unemployment  3.0 (direct) and  3.0 (equation 8)
floor 12: wage 12.0, employment 48.0, unemployment  6.0 (direct) and  6.0 (equation 8)
floor 14: wage 14.0, employment 46.0, unemployment 12.0 (direct) and 12.0 (equation 8)

Check 3: compound growth. We let GDP per person grow by 1.9 percent a year for 155 years, one year at a time, and compare the result with equation (3). Then equation (4) must recover the growth rate, and the log formula must come close.

Python note. range(155) counts 0, 1, …, 154, so the for loop runs its indented line 155 times. level = level * (1 + 0.019) replaces the old value by the new one. The underscore _ is a name for a loop counter that we do not need.

level = 1.0
for _ in range(155):
    level = level * (1 + 0.019)                              # one year of growth
print(f"Year by year: level after 155 years = {level:.3f}")
print(f"Equation (3): (1.019)^155           = {(1 + 0.019) ** 155:.3f}")
print(f"Equation (4) recovers g             = {100 * average_growth(1.0, level, 155):.3f}%")
print(f"Log formula (ln y_T - ln y_0) / T   = {100 * (np.log(level) - np.log(1.0)) / 155:.3f}%")
print(f"Tenfold in 100 years needs g        = {100 * average_growth(1, 10, 100):.2f}%")
Year by year: level after 155 years = 18.493
Equation (3): (1.019)^155           = 18.493
Equation (4) recovers g             = 1.900%
Log formula (ln y_T - ln y_0) / T   = 1.882%
Tenfold in 100 years needs g        = 2.33%

Check 4: the rule of 70. Equation (5) against the exact doubling time, and the factor after 100 years, as in the table above.

for g in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10):
    print(f"g = {100 * g:4.1f}%: doubles in {doubling_time(g):5.1f} years (rule of 70: {70 / (100 * g):5.1f}); "
          f"factor after 100 years {(1 + g) ** 100:7.1f}")
g =  1.0%: doubles in  69.7 years (rule of 70:  70.0); factor after 100 years     2.7
g =  2.0%: doubles in  35.0 years (rule of 70:  35.0); factor after 100 years     7.2
g =  3.0%: doubles in  23.4 years (rule of 70:  23.3); factor after 100 years    19.2
g =  5.0%: doubles in  14.2 years (rule of 70:  14.0); factor after 100 years   131.5
g = 10.0%: doubles in   7.3 years (rule of 70:   7.0); factor after 100 years 13780.6

Check 5: two labor-market ratios. We plug the February and April 2020 values into both sides of equation (1). Then we split the fall of \(e\) into its two parts with logs.

Pop, LF = 100.0, 63.3                            # per 100 adults, February 2020: 63.3 in the labor force
U = 0.035 * LF                                   # 3.5 percent of the labor force is unemployed
e_feb = 100 * (LF - U) / Pop                     # left side of equation (1): E / Pop, in percent
print(f"February 2020: E/Pop = {e_feb:.2f}%,   p(1 - u) = {63.3 * (1 - 0.035):.2f}%")
e_apr = 60.1 * (1 - 0.148)                       # equation (1) for April 2020
fall = np.log(e_apr) - np.log(e_feb)
part_p = np.log(60.1) - np.log(63.3)             # participation part
part_u = np.log(1 - 0.148) - np.log(1 - 0.035)   # unemployment part
print(f"April 2020:    e = {e_apr:.1f}%, a fall of {e_feb - e_apr:.1f} points")
print(f"Share of the log fall due to participation: {part_p / fall:.0%}, to unemployment: {part_u / fall:.0%}")
print(f"The two parts add up: {part_p + part_u:.4f} = {fall:.4f}")
February 2020: E/Pop = 61.08%,   p(1 - u) = 61.08%
April 2020:    e = 51.2%, a fall of 9.9 points
Share of the log fall due to participation: 29%, to unemployment: 71%
The two parts add up: -0.1764 = -0.1764

Check 6: compounding prices and the log form of the gap. A year of 3,080 percent inflation, two years of 10 percent, and equation (2) against its log form for small and large gaps.

print(f"3,080% inflation multiplies prices by {1 + 3080 / 100:.1f}")
print(f"Two years of 10% raise prices by {100 * ((1 + 0.10) * (1 + 0.10) - 1):.0f}%")
for ratio_to_potential in (0.953, 0.83, 1.23):
    exact = 100 * (ratio_to_potential - 1)                   # equation (2)
    approx = 100 * np.log(ratio_to_potential)                # log form
    print(f"Y / Y_pot = {ratio_to_potential:.3f}: gap {exact:+6.1f}% (equation 2), {approx:+6.1f}% (log form)")
3,080% inflation multiplies prices by 31.8
Two years of 10% raise prices by 21%
Y / Y_pot = 0.953: gap   -4.7% (equation 2),   -4.8% (log form)
Y / Y_pot = 0.830: gap  -17.0% (equation 2),  -18.6% (log form)
Y / Y_pot = 1.230: gap  +23.0% (equation 2),  +20.7% (log form)

The log form is within a tenth of a point for a gap like 2009’s, but it is off by almost 2 points for the Great Depression’s 17 percent, and by more than 2 for the wartime boom of 1944.

Income over time and across countries

The first big fact of macroeconomics is how unequal incomes are, both across countries and across time. We compare GDP per person for six economies and for many more.

Fig. 1: GDP per person in six countries

Goal. Document the first big fact of macroeconomics: income differs enormously across countries and over time.

The data come from the Maddison Project, which estimates GDP per person for every country over long periods. GDP (gross domestic product) is the overall income of a country; Chapter 2 explains how it is measured. All values are in 2022 dollars, so they can be compared across years.

Python note. pd.read_csv(...) reads a data file into a DataFrame, a table with named columns. DATA_URL + "fig1-1.csv" glues the folder address and the file name together. .head() shows the first five rows.

six = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-1.csv")
six.head()

The table is wide: one column per country, and only the benchmark years the textbook uses (1870, 1890, 1900, 1929 and every decade from 1950). Plotly Express prefers long tables, with one row per country and year.

Python note. .melt(id_vars="year") turns the country columns into rows: the old column names go into a new column (var_name) and the numbers into another (value_name). A dictionary such as NAMES pairs keys with values, and .map(NAMES) replaces each column name with a readable country name.

NAMES = {"gdppc_usa": "United States", "gdppc_gbr": "United Kingdom", "gdppc_jpn": "Japan",
         "gdppc_arg": "Argentina", "gdppc_zaf": "South Africa", "gdppc_chn": "China"}
long = six.melt(id_vars="year", var_name="series", value_name="gdppc")
long["country"] = long.series.map(NAMES)

Beyond the textbook’s six countries

The Maddison Project covers far more than six countries. The file maddison_world.csv holds all of them, already in long form and in the same 2022 dollars, for every year with an estimate. A second file, countries.csv, lists every economy with its world region and its membership of the G7, the G20 and the OECD. Every data figure of this notebook uses it.

world = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_world.csv")
countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
print(f"{world.country.nunique()} countries, {world.year.min()}-{world.year.max()}, {len(world):,} rows")
world.head()

Before we use a new file, we check that it agrees with the one we trust. For the six countries at the benchmark years, the two files should hold exactly the same numbers.

Python note. .isin(list) is True for the rows whose value is in the list. .merge(other, on=[...]) joins two tables, matching rows with the same year and country; columns with the same name get the endings _x and _y.

BENCHMARKS = list(six.year)                          # the textbook's benchmark years
on_benchmarks = world[world.year.isin(BENCHMARKS)]
check = long.merge(on_benchmarks, on=["year", "country"])
print(f"{len(check)} matching rows, largest difference: {(check.gdppc_x - check.gdppc_y).abs().max()} dollars")
78 matching rows, largest difference: 0 dollars

Every country keeps the same color in every figure. The textbook’s countries get fixed colors of our palette, and each of the other countries one of 24 distinct colors.

Python note. for i, name in enumerate(...) hands over each name together with its position i (0, 1, 2, …). i % 24 is the remainder after dividing by 24, so the 24 colors repeat in turn. if name not in COLORS: skips the names that already have a color.

COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "United Kingdom": TEAL, "Japan": GREEN, "Argentina": "#5aa0d8",
          "South Africa": "#0b4f47", "China": "#e0a33b", "Euro area": "#7b5ea7", "Europe": "#7b5ea7"}
OTHER = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24                 # 24 distinct colors for the other countries
for i, name in enumerate(countries.country):
    if name not in COLORS:
        COLORS[name] = OTHER[i % len(OTHER)]

The textbook draws this figure on a ratio scale: each step up the vertical axis doubles the value (1,000, 2,000, 4,000, …). Equal distances then mean equal percentage changes, so a country growing at a steady rate draws a straight line (the log form of equation 3). Chapter 3 explains ratio scales in detail.

Python note. px.line draws one line per value of color=, and color_discrete_map=COLORS fixes each country’s color. log_y=True gives a ratio scale, and tickvals sets the numbers printed on the axis (Plotly’s own labels are hard to read on a ratio scale). On a ratio scale, the axis range is given in powers of ten: np.log10(800). The if ... else blocks run one branch or the other: here they widen the axis, in one step, when a chosen country is very poor or very rich, and x if condition else y picks x when the condition is true. set(chosen) - set(data.country) keeps the chosen names that have no data, and ", ".join(missing) writes them in one line, separated by commas.

BOOK = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Japan", "Argentina", "South Africa", "China")
TICKS = [500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000]


def gdp_per_person(scale="ratio", chosen=BOOK):
    """Fig. 1.1: GDP per person at the textbook's benchmark years, 1870-2022 (2022 dollars)."""
    data = on_benchmarks[on_benchmarks.country.isin(chosen)]
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    title = "2022: U.S. income per person 5× South Africa's; China's up 24-fold since 1950"
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", hover_name="country", markers=True,
                  log_y=(scale == "ratio"), color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  title=title, labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "country": "Country"})
    low = 800 if data.gdppc.min() >= 800 else 400              # a very poor country: one step lower
    high = 90000 if data.gdppc.max() <= 90000 else 250000      # a very rich country: one step higher
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=TICKS, range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    else:
        fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, high - 10000])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2027])
    return fig

Python note. interact calls a function and redraws its figure every time you change a control. ToggleButtons gives one button per option. SelectMultiple is a list from which you can pick several entries: hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and click to add or remove a country. The ; at the end only hides an extra line of text.

interact(gdp_per_person,
         scale=ToggleButtons(options=["ratio", "linear"], value="ratio", description="vertical scale"),
         chosen=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value=BOOK, rows=8, description="countries"));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with buttons for the vertical scale and a menu of countries
fig = gdp_per_person()
fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0.01, y=0.98, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", buttons=[
    dict(label="ratio scale", method="relayout", args=[{"yaxis.type": "log", "yaxis.autorange": True, "yaxis.tickvals": TICKS}]),
    dict(label="linear scale", method="relayout", args=[{"yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.autorange": True, "yaxis.tickvals": None}])])])
extra = country_traces(on_benchmarks, "gdppc", BOOK, fmt=",.0f", markers=True)
country_menu(fig, extra, countries)

Sources. Data: Maddison Project Database 2023, GDP per capita (gdppc), Groningen Growth and Development Centre (Bolt and van Zanden 2024, doi:10.34894/INZBF2), converted from 2011 to 2022 dollars with the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis GDP deflator (A191RD3A086NBEA), via FRED. Country groups: World Bank country classifications. Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-1.csv, data/ch01/maddison_world.csv and data/ch01/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries; click a country in the legend to hide it, or double-click to show it alone.

What to notice.

  • In every year, the richest of the six countries has several times the income of the poorest. In 2022 the United States leads and South Africa is last.
  • The U.K. was richer than the United States in 1870 and 1890; by 1900 the United States was ahead.
  • Japan’s income fell between 1929 and 1950 (World War II) and then rose very fast: it passed South Africa in the 1950s and Argentina in the 1960s. China was almost flat until 1950 and has grown fast since, passing Argentina by 2020.
  • Switch to the linear scale: the lines for poorer countries are squeezed near zero, and the early growth of every country becomes invisible. That is why the textbook uses a ratio scale.
  • Add South Korea: with 1,288 dollars per person in 1950 it was poorer than Japan was in 1870. It grew so fast that by 2020 it had passed Japan. Many countries have no estimate before 1950, so their lines start there.

Key numbers: how much richer?

The textbook asks why the typical American is “more than 10 times richer” than a century ago and “25 times richer” than the typical Ethiopian. A wider file holds every available year for the six countries and for Ethiopia, so we can check both numbers.

Python note. .pivot(index="year", columns="iso3", values="gdppc") turns a long table back into a wide one, with the years as row labels and one column per country code. Then wide.loc[2022, "ETH"] picks one number, and us[us < x] keeps only the years in which the condition is true.

annual = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_annual.csv")
wide = annual.pivot(index="year", columns="iso3", values="gdppc")
us = wide["USA"]
print(f"U.S. 2022 / U.S. 1922:  {us[2022] / us[1922]:.1f}")
print(f"Last year with less than a tenth of the 2022 income: {us[us < us[2022] / 10].index.max()}")
print(f"U.S. / Ethiopia, 2022:  {us[2022] / wide.loc[2022, 'ETH']:.1f}")
print("U.S. / Ethiopia in other years:")
print((us / wide["ETH"]).loc[[1950, 1980, 2000, 2010, 2022]].round(1))
U.S. 2022 / U.S. 1922:  5.8
Last year with less than a tenth of the 2022 income: 1879
U.S. / Ethiopia, 2022:  25.5
U.S. / Ethiopia in other years:
year
1950    24.5
1980    28.7
2000    59.4
2010    44.5
2022    25.5
dtype: float64

The 25-fold gap with Ethiopia is confirmed: in 2022 the ratio is about 25.5. The “10 times richer than a century ago” is not: in the current Maddison data, U.S. income in 2022 is about 5.8 times its 1922 level. A tenfold gap takes us back to 1879, about 140 years. (Fig. 7 checks the same claim with a different data source.) Notice too that the gap with Ethiopia was much larger around 2000 (about 59 times); the textbook’s later mention of a “50-fold” gap fits those years. Ethiopia has grown fast since then. Always check a claim against the data, and say which data and which year you used.

Your turn. By what factor did GDP per person rise between 1950 and 2022 in Japan? And in the United States? Use the wide table.

Hint

Divide wide.loc[2022, "JPN"] by wide.loc[1950, "JPN"], then do the same with "USA". Fast growth from a low starting point is called catch-up; Chapter 5 explains it.

Recessions, inflation and unemployment

Next come three facts about how economies move from year to year: jobs lost in recessions, bursts of inflation, and lasting differences in unemployment.

Fig. 2: The U.S. employment-population ratio

Goal. See how recessions show up in the labor market.

The employment-population ratio is the percentage of the adult population that has a job. It is monthly data, so we tell pandas that the date column holds dates. A second small file lists the start (peak) and end (trough) month of every U.S. recession since 1960, as dated by the NBER.

Python note. parse_dates=["date"] turns text such as "2020-04-01" into real dates, so that Plotly and pandas can work with them. .tail() shows the last five rows.

emp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-2.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
recessions = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "recessions.csv", parse_dates=["peak", "trough"])
emp.tail()
date emp_pop_ratio
795 2026-05-01 59.2
796 2026-06-01 59.0
797 2026-07-01 58.9
798 2026-08-01 59.1
799 2026-09-01 59.2

Look at the dates in the last rows: September 2025 is followed by November 2025. A whole month is missing. Let us check how many months should be there.

Python note. pd.date_range(..., freq="MS") lists the first day of every month between two dates. months.isin(emp.date) is True for each month that appears in the data, and ~ turns True into False and back, so months[~ ...] keeps the months that are missing.

months = pd.date_range("1960-01-01", "2026-09-01", freq="MS")
missing = months[~months.isin(emp.date)]
print(f"{len(emp)} rows of data for {len(months)} months. Missing: {list(missing.strftime('%Y-%m'))}")
800 rows of data for 801 months. Missing: ['2025-10']

October 2025 is missing because the Bureau of Labor Statistics did not collect its survey during the federal government shutdown of that autumn. The chart simply joins September and November. Gaps like this are common in real data, which is why we check before we compute.

Python note. The shaded bands are the recessions. A for loop repeats the indented line once for each recession: zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough) hands over one (peak, trough) pair at a time, and fig.add_vrect shades the band between the two dates. rangeslider_visible=True adds a small copy of the chart below the axis: drag its handles to zoom in on a period.

fig = px.line(emp, x="date", y="emp_pop_ratio",
              labels={"date": "Year", "emp_pop_ratio": "Employment-population ratio (percent)"},
              title="The ratio fell 4.5 points in 2007–09 and 9.9 points in the Covid-19 recession")
fig.update_traces(line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2))
for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
    fig.add_vrect(x0=peak, x1=trough, fillcolor=BLUE, opacity=0.12, line_width=0)
fig.update_yaxes(range=[50, 66], tickvals=[52, 54, 56, 58, 60, 62, 64, 66])   # no label in the bottom-left corner
fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True)
fig.show()

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey, Employment-Population Ratio (EMRATIO), via FRED; recession dates: NBER business cycle dates, as in the NBER-based recession indicator (USREC), via FRED. Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-2.csv and data/ch01/recessions.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The ratio rose from about 56 percent in the early 1960s to a peak of 64.7 percent in April 2000.
  • It falls in every recession (the shaded bands), but the last two falls are far deeper than the others: the 2007–09 recession and the Covid-19 collapse of spring 2020.
  • After 2009 the recovery was slow. After the Covid drop the ratio bounced back within two years, but it has not returned to its February 2020 level of 61.1 percent.

Key numbers: how deep was each fall?

The textbook says that the two latest recessions brought the sharpest declines in employment in more than 50 years. For each recession, we compare the ratio in the peak month with its lowest value up to two years after the trough (employment often keeps falling after a recession ends).

Python note. set_index("date") uses the dates as row labels, so ratio[:peak] keeps every month up to the peak and .iloc[-1] takes the last of them. pd.DateOffset(years=2) adds two years to a date. Each pass of the loop adds one row to the list falls, which becomes a DataFrame at the end.

ratio = emp.set_index("date").emp_pop_ratio
falls = []
for peak, trough in zip(recessions.peak, recessions.trough):
    at_peak = ratio[:peak].iloc[-1]
    lowest = ratio[peak:trough + pd.DateOffset(years=2)].min()
    falls.append([peak.strftime("%Y-%m"), at_peak, lowest, at_peak - lowest])
pd.DataFrame(falls, columns=["Recession peak", "Ratio at peak", "Lowest after", "Fall (points)"]).round(1)
Recession peak Ratio at peak Lowest after Fall (points)
0 1960-04 56.4 55.0 1.4
1 1969-12 58.1 56.2 1.9
2 1973-11 58.2 55.8 2.4
3 1980-01 60.0 57.7 2.3
4 1981-07 59.1 57.1 2.0
5 1990-07 62.8 61.2 1.6
6 2001-03 64.3 62.0 2.3
7 2007-12 62.7 58.2 4.5
8 2020-02 61.1 51.2 9.9

Before 2007, no recession lowered the ratio by more than 2.4 points. The 2007–09 recession lowered it by 4.5 points and the Covid-19 recession by 9.9 points, from 61.1 to 51.2 percent in just two months. The textbook’s claim holds.

Beyond the United States: employment around the world

The International Labour Organization (ILO) estimates the employment-population ratio for almost every country, once a year since 1991, and the World Bank publishes these estimates. The concept is the same as in the textbook’s figure, with one difference: the ILO counts adults from age 15, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics from age 16. Let us see how much that matters for the United States.

Python note. emp.date.dt.year takes the year of each date, and groupby(...).mean() averages the months of each year. Subtracting two Series matches their rows by year.

employment = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "employment_world.csv")
us_yearly = emp.groupby(emp.date.dt.year).emp_pop_ratio.mean()
ilo_us = employment[employment.country == "United States"].set_index("year").emp_pop_ratio
print(f"{employment.country.nunique()} countries, {employment.year.min()}-{employment.year.max()}")
print("ILO (ages 15+) minus BLS (ages 16+), U.S., percentage points:")
print((ilo_us - us_yearly).dropna().round(1).loc[[1991, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2025]])
188 countries, 1991-2025
ILO (ages 15+) minus BLS (ages 16+), U.S., percentage points:
1991   -1.1
2000   -0.9
2010   -0.9
2020   -0.2
2025   -0.7
Name: emp_pop_ratio, dtype: float64

The two U.S. series differ by about one point or less, because the ILO also counts 15-year-olds, few of whom work. The ups and downs are the same, so we can compare countries with the ILO series.

def employment_chart(chosen=("United States",)):
    """Fig. 1.2 for many countries: employment-population ratio, ages 15+, 1991-2025 (ILO estimates)."""
    data = employment[employment.country.isin(chosen)]
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    title = "Employment-population ratio, ages 15 and over (ILO estimates)"
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="emp_pop_ratio", color="country", hover_name="country",
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)}, title=title,
                  labels={"year": "Year", "emp_pop_ratio": "Employment-population ratio (percent)", "country": "Country"})
    low = 40 if data.emp_pop_ratio.min() >= 40 else 10      # widen the axis in one step if needed
    high = 70 if data.emp_pop_ratio.max() <= 70 else 90
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1990, 2026])
    return fig
interact(employment_chart,
         chosen=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(employment.country.unique()), value=("United States",), rows=8,
                               description="countries"));
Show the code of the website version

fig = employment_chart()
country_menu(fig, country_traces(employment, "emp_pop_ratio", ["United States"]), countries)

Sources. Data: International Labour Organization modelled estimates, Employment to population ratio, 15+ (SL.EMP.TOTL.SP.ZS), via the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. Country groups: World Bank country classifications. Prepared files: data/ch01/employment_world.csv and data/ch01/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries; click a country in the legend to hide it.

  • Add Germany and Japan. In 2020 the U.S. ratio (ILO, yearly) fell by 3.9 points, Germany’s by only 1.2 and Japan’s by 0.3. Both countries paid firms to keep workers on reduced hours instead of laying them off, so the Covid-19 recession cost far fewer jobs there.
  • Germany’s ratio rose from 53.9 percent in 2007 to 59.4 percent in 2019, while the U.S. ratio fell from 62.0 to 60.5 percent: a recession is not the only thing that moves employment.
  • Ratios differ a lot across countries, from below 30 percent (e.g. Yemen) to above 80 percent (e.g. Tanzania, Qatar). Low ratios often mean that few women work for pay; very high ones often mean that people cannot afford not to work. These numbers are model-based ILO estimates, so read single years for poor countries with care.

Goal. Document the history of inflation in four rich economies.

The inflation rate is the percentage change in consumer prices over a year. The file fig1-3.csv has one column per economy, for the textbook’s four. We rename the columns, because we will use this table to average inflation over eras below.

Python note. .rename(columns={old: new}) changes column names.

inflation = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-3.csv")

The World Bank’s main database (WDI) has no Argentine inflation before 2018: from 2007 to 2015 the official price index was widely judged to understate inflation. For such gaps the file uses the World Bank’s Global Inflation Database (GID), which collects the best available estimates. Always look at where a number comes from.

The chart below draws the chosen economies. The vertical axis runs from −5 to 25 percent, and it is widened in steps (to 50, 100, … percent) when a chosen country had higher inflation. add_hline draws a horizontal line, here a dashed zero line: below it, prices fall (deflation).

Python note. for top in [...]: tries the steps in order, and break leaves the loop at the first step that is high enough. data.inflation.idxmax() is the row label of the highest inflation, and data.loc[row] reads that row.

BOOK_INFLATION = ("United States", "United Kingdom", "Euro area", "Japan")


def inflation_chart(chosen=BOOK_INFLATION):
    """Fig. 1.3: CPI inflation, 1960-2025, for the chosen economies."""
    data = world_inflation[world_inflation.country.isin(chosen)]
    for top in [25, 50, 100, 250, 1000, 5000, 25000, 100000]:  # widen the axis in steps
        if data.inflation.max() <= top:
            break
    title = "Inflation peaked in the 1970s (24% in the U.K.) and surged again in 2021–22"
    if set(chosen) != set(BOOK_INFLATION) and len(data) > 0:
        row = data.loc[data.inflation.idxmax()]
        title = f"Highest inflation shown: {row.country}, {row.inflation:,.1f}% in {row.year}"
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="inflation", color="country", hover_name="country", title=title,
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "inflation": "Inflation rate (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[min(-5, data.inflation.min() - 2), top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig
interact(inflation_chart,
         chosen=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world_inflation.country.unique()), value=BOOK_INFLATION, rows=8,
                               description="economies"));

Data: World Bank, World Development Indicators, Inflation, consumer prices (FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG), also via FRED for the United Kingdom (FPCPITOTLZGGBR), the euro area (FPCPITOTLZGEMU) and Japan (FPCPITOTLZGJPN); United States: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPIAUCNS), via FRED; gaps filled from the World Bank’s Global Inflation Database (Ha, Kose and Ohnsorge). Country groups: World Bank country classifications. Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-3.csv, data/ch01/inflation_world.csv and data/ch01/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.3 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries; click a name in the legend to hide that line, or double-click it to show it alone.

What to notice.

  • Inflation peaked in the 1970s: Japan at 23 percent in 1974, the U.K. at 24 percent in 1975, the United States at 13.5 percent in 1980.
  • From the mid-1990s to 2019, inflation was low and stable everywhere, and Japan often had deflation.
  • In 2021–2022 inflation jumped in all four economies. Hover over 2022 to compare them.
  • Add Germany: its inflation peaked at only 7.0 percent in 1973, about as high as in 2022 (6.9 percent). Add Argentina: the axis jumps to 5,000 percent, because prices rose 3,080 percent in 1989 (hyperinflation); prices were almost stable from 1995 to 2001, and inflation was back above 100 percent in 2023–24.

Key numbers: three eras of inflation

To check the caption’s story, we average inflation over eras.

Python note. pd.cut sorts each year into a bin: the years from 1960 to 1969 get the label "1960s", and so on (each bin includes its right edge). groupby("era").mean() then averages every column within each era.

inflation["era"] = pd.cut(inflation.year, bins=[1959, 1969, 1979, 1989, 2019, 2020, 2025],
                          labels=["1960s", "1970s", "1980s", "1990-2019", "2020", "2021-2025"])
inflation.groupby("era", observed=True)[["U.S.", "U.K.", "Euro area", "Japan"]].mean().round(1) + 0.0   # + 0.0 avoids "-0.0"
U.S. U.K. Euro area Japan
era
1960s 2.3 3.5 2.9 5.3
1970s 7.1 12.6 8.5 9.0
1980s 5.6 7.2 6.8 2.5
1990-2019 2.4 2.5 2.6 0.5
2020 1.2 1.0 0.2 0.0
2021-2025 4.5 4.9 4.3 2.3

Average inflation in the 1970s ranged from about 7 percent (United States) to almost 13 percent (U.K.). From 1990 to 2019 it averaged about 2.5 percent in the United States, the U.K. and the euro area, and 0.5 percent in Japan. It then rose again after 2020. In our data, U.S. inflation in 2022 was 8.0 percent, higher than the 6.4 percent the textbook shows, probably because the full-year figure was not yet available when the book was written.

Fig. 4: The unemployment rate in the U.S., Europe and Japan

Goal. Compare unemployment across three large economies, and test a claim about Europe.

The unemployment rate is the share of the labor force (people who have a job or are looking for one) that is looking for work but does not have a job. “Europe” here is the euro area of 12 countries, from the European Commission’s AMECO database; it starts in 1960.

The empty cells (NaN, “not a number”) in the Europe column are the years 1955–1959, before the series starts. pandas skips them when it computes averages.

Other countries publish unemployment rates too. unemployment_world.csv holds the textbook’s three series (copied from fig1-4.csv), the European Commission’s AMECO series for 40 other mostly European and rich countries (from 1960), and ILO estimates from the World Bank for the other OECD and G20 members (from 1991). All follow the same international (ILO) definition of unemployment.

world_unemp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "unemployment_world.csv")
world_unemp.groupby("source").country.nunique()
source

Name: country, dtype: int64

The textbook says that over the past two decades unemployment has been “nearly twice as high in Europe as in the United States” (Jones 2024). The function below draws the chosen economies, shades a period, and computes the average ratio of the European rate to the U.S. rate in that period. The vertical axis runs to 14 percent, and to 30 or 40 percent when a chosen country had higher unemployment.

Python note. start, end = period unpacks a pair of numbers into two variables. unemp[(unemp.year >= start) & (unemp.year <= end)] keeps the rows where both conditions are true; & means “and”, and each condition needs its own brackets.

BOOK_UNEMP = ("United States", "Europe", "Japan")


def unemployment_chart(period=(2006, 2025), chosen=BOOK_UNEMP):
    """Fig. 1.4: unemployment rates, with the average Europe/U.S. ratio over a shaded period."""
    start, end = period
    chosen_years = unemp[(unemp.year >= start) & (unemp.year <= end)]
    ratio = (chosen_years["Europe"] / chosen_years["United States"]).mean()
    data = world_unemp[world_unemp.country.isin(chosen)]
    title = f"{start}–{end}: Europe's rate was {ratio:.2f} times the U.S. rate on average"
    missing = sorted(set(chosen) - set(data.country))
    if missing:
        title = "No data for " + ", ".join(missing)
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y="unrate", color="country", hover_name="country", title=title,
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(chosen)},
                  labels={"year": "Year", "unrate": "Unemployment rate (percent)", "country": "Economy"})
    fig.add_vrect(x0=start, x1=end, fillcolor=GRAY, opacity=0.15, line_width=0)
    top = 14 if data.unrate.max() <= 14 else (30 if data.unrate.max() <= 30 else 40)   # widen in steps
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[0, top])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1954, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig

Python note. An IntRangeSlider has two handles, so it chooses a whole period at once.

interact(unemployment_chart,
         period=IntRangeSlider(value=(2006, 2025), min=1960, max=2025, step=1, description="period", style=WIDE),
         chosen=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(world_unemp.country.unique()), value=BOOK_UNEMP, rows=8,
                               description="economies"));

Country groups: World Bank country classifications. Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-4.csv, data/ch01/unemployment_world.csv and data/ch01/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.4 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, the menu above the chart adds a group of countries; click a country in the legend to hide it.

What to notice.

  • Over the last 20 years (2006–2025), European unemployment was on average about 1.6 times the U.S. rate: much higher, though a bit less than “nearly twice”.
  • From 1960 to 1978 Europe’s rate was below the U.S. rate every year, on average just over half of it. Choose the period 1960–1979 to see it.
  • Japan’s unemployment rate stayed low throughout, never above 5.4 percent.
  • “Europe” hides large differences. Add Spain and Greece: both passed 26 percent in 2013, after the euro-area debt crisis. Add Germany: its rate fell from 10.5 percent in 2005 to 3.8 percent in 2025, below the U.S. rate.

Key numbers: when did Europe overtake the United States?

above = unemp[unemp["Europe"] > unemp["United States"]]

      f"Japan {unemp['Japan'].max():.1f} ({unemp.loc[unemp['Japan'].idxmax(), 'year']})")
First year with higher unemployment in Europe: 1979
Highest rates: U.S. 9.7 (1982), Europe 12.1 (2013), Japan 5.4 (2002)

Europe first overtook the United States in 1979. The two rates crossed back and forth in the early 1980s; from 1984 on, Europe was higher in every year except 2020, when the Covid-19 shock sent U.S. unemployment to 8.1 percent.

Budget and trade deficits

Two deficits often make the news: the government spending more than it collects, and a country buying more from abroad than it sells. Here we look at both for the United States.

Fig. 5: Budget and trade deficits in the United States

Goal. Look at two deficits that often appear in the news.

The budget deficit is what the federal government spends beyond its revenue, and the trade deficit is what the country imports beyond its exports. Both are measured as a percentage of GDP, so that years with very different GDP can be compared. A negative deficit is a surplus.

deficits = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-5.csv")
deficits = deficits.rename(columns={"budget_deficit_pct_gdp": "Budget deficit", "trade_deficit_pct_gdp": "Trade deficit"})
deficits.tail(3)
year Budget deficit Trade deficit
63 2023 6.09529 2.74172
64 2024 6.47374 3.00009
65 2025 5.76103 2.98500

deficits_world.csv has the same two deficits for about 200 countries. Its U.S. rows are the textbook’s (the federal budget). For the other countries the budget deficit is that of the general government (federal, state and local governments together), from the IMF, and the trade deficit comes from the World Bank; IMF budget data start around 1980–2000. For the United States, the general-government deficit averaged about 1.2 points of GDP more than the federal one in 2001–2025, partly because states and cities borrow too. Keep this difference in mind when you compare countries.

world_deficits = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "deficits_world.csv")
world_deficits[world_deficits.country == "Germany"].tail(3)
iso3 country year budget_deficit trade_deficit source
3555 DEU Germany 2023 2.2 -3.97 IMF WEO + WDI
3556 DEU Germany 2024 2.7 -3.78 IMF WEO + WDI
3557 DEU Germany 2025 2.9 -2.36 IMF WEO + WDI

Python note. A Dropdown is a menu from which you choose one entry, here one country. np.floor and np.ceil round down and up, so 5 * np.ceil(x / 5) is the next multiple of 5 above x: the axis grows in steps of 5 points when a country’s deficits are large.

def deficits_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 1.5 for one country: budget and trade deficits, percent of GDP (negative = surplus)."""
    data = world_deficits[world_deficits.country == country]
    data = data.rename(columns={"budget_deficit": "Budget deficit", "trade_deficit": "Trade deficit"})
    title = f"{country}: budget deficit (general government) and trade deficit"
    if country == "United States":
        title = "U.S. budget deficit near 14% of GDP in 2020; trade deficit peaked in 2006"
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=["Budget deficit", "Trade deficit"], color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Percent of GDP", "variable": "Deficit"}, title=title)
    fig.add_hline(y=0, line_dash="dash", line_color=GRAY)
    values = data[["Budget deficit", "Trade deficit"]]
    low = min(-5, 5 * np.floor(values.min().min() / 5))
    high = max(15, 5 * np.ceil(values.max().max() / 5))
    fig.update_yaxes(range=[low, high])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1959, 2026])
    fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
    return fig
interact(deficits_chart,
         country=Dropdown(options=sorted(world_deficits.country.unique()), value="United States", description="country"));

Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, national accounts, via FRED: federal government net saving (FGDEF), net exports (NETEXP) and GDP (GDP); other countries: IMF, World Economic Outlook, general government net lending/borrowing (GGXCNL_NGDP) and World Bank, World Development Indicators, External balance on goods and services (NE.RSB.GNFS.ZS). Country groups: World Bank country classifications. Prepared files: data/ch01/fig1-5.csv, data/ch01/deficits_world.csv and data/ch01/countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 1.5 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

The website’s menu lists the G20 and OECD members; in Colab you can choose any of the countries.

What to notice.

  • The budget deficit jumps in recessions (1975, the early 1980s, 2009–2010) and above all in 2020, when it reached almost 14 percent of GDP.
  • The trade deficit was near zero, usually a small surplus, until the mid-1970s. It peaked in 2006 at 5.7 percent of GDP.
  • In 2025 the budget deficit was still about 5.8 percent of GDP and the trade deficit about 3 percent.
  • Choose Germany: it runs trade surpluses (negative deficits), 7.4 percent of GDP in 2015. Its budget deficit of 9.4 percent in 1995 is an accounting event, not a spending spree: that year the government took over the debts of the agency that had privatized East German firms. Choose Greece: a budget deficit of 15.4 percent of GDP in 2009 started its debt crisis.

Key numbers: surpluses and record deficits

Python note. deficits[deficits["Budget deficit"] < 0] keeps the rows with a budget surplus, and .year.tolist() lists their years. .idxmax() gives the row label of the largest value, and .loc[row, column] reads one cell.

What a model does

With the facts in hand, we turn to the tool that explains them. A small live model shows how inputs go in and outcomes come out.

Fig. 6: The structure of economic models

Goal. See what a model does: it takes inputs and determines outcomes.

Every economic model has the same structure. The model builder picks the inputs:

  • parameters, fixed numbers such as \(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{\ell}\), \(\bar{f}\), or a minimum wage set by law;
  • exogenous variables, inputs that may change over time in a way the model builder decides in advance, such as the number of people in the economy.

The model, a set of equations, then determines the endogenous variables, here the wage and employment. The textbook draws this as three boxes: inputs → MODEL → outcomes. Below, the boxes are live: every slider is an input, and the right box shows the outcomes the model computes.

We add one input the textbook mentions as an example of a parameter: a minimum wage. If it is below \(w^*\), it has no effect. If it is above \(w^*\), the wage equals the minimum wage, firms hire only the hours they demand at that wage, and the hours that workers offer but cannot sell are unemployment, \(L^s - L^d\), which is equation (8) of the Model overview. (Think of \(\bar{\ell}\) as growing with the number of people in the economy: more people offer more hours at any wage.)

Python note. fig.add_shape(type="rect", ...) draws a rectangle and fig.add_annotation(...) writes text; <br> starts a new line and <b>...</b> makes text bold. An annotation with showarrow=True draws an arrow from (ax, ay) to (x, y). max(w_star, w_min) is the larger of the two numbers. The loops run once per box and once per arrow.

def structure_of_models(a=2.0, l=30.0, f=60.0, w_min=0.0):
    """Fig. 1.6 as a live model: inputs (parameters) -> MODEL -> outcomes (endogenous variables)."""
    w_star, L_star = equilibrium(a, l, f)
    w = max(w_star, w_min)                         # a minimum wage above w* sets the wage
    L = labor_demand(w, f)                         # firms hire the hours they demand at that wage
    unemployed = max(labor_supply(w, a, l) - L, 0.0)   # hours offered but not hired (zero, not -0.00, if w = w*)
    inputs = (f"<b>INPUTS</b><br><i>parameters and exogenous<br>variables</i><br><br>supply slope a = {a:.1f}"
              f"<br>hours at zero wage l = {l:.0f}<br>demand at zero wage f = {f:.0f}<br>minimum wage = {w_min:.0f}")
    model = "<b>MODEL</b><br><br>Lˢ = a·w + l<br>Lᵈ = f − w<br>Lˢ = Lᵈ, unless<br>a minimum wage<br>is above w*"
    outcomes = (f"<b>OUTCOMES</b><br><i>endogenous variables</i><br><br>wage w = {w:.2f}"
                f"<br>employment L = {L:.2f}<br>unemployment = {unemployed:.2f}")
    fig = go.Figure()
    for x0, x1, text in [[0.0, 0.33, inputs], [0.39, 0.61, model], [0.67, 1.0, outcomes]]:
        fig.add_shape(type="rect", x0=x0, x1=x1, y0=0.12, y1=0.88, fillcolor="#ecf3fa", line=dict(color=BLUE))
        fig.add_annotation(x=(x0 + x1) / 2, y=0.5, text=text, showarrow=False, font=dict(size=13))
    for x_from, x_to in [[0.33, 0.39], [0.61, 0.67]]:
        fig.add_annotation(x=x_to, y=0.5, ax=x_from, ay=0.5, xref="x", yref="y", axref="x", ayref="y",
                           text="", showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=4, arrowcolor=GREEN)
    fig.update_xaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_yaxes(visible=False, range=[0, 1])
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Inputs → model → outcomes: wage w = {w:.2f}, employment L = {L:.2f}")
    return fig

Python note. A FloatSlider chooses a number between min and max in steps of step. value is where it starts: the textbook’s numbers.

interact(structure_of_models,
         a=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=1.0, max=4.0, step=0.5, description="supply slope a", style=WIDE),
         l=FloatSlider(value=30, min=20, max=40, step=5, description="hours at zero wage l", style=WIDE),
         f=FloatSlider(value=60, min=50, max=70, step=5, description="demand at zero wage f", style=WIDE),
         w_min=FloatSlider(value=0, min=0, max=20, step=1, description="minimum wage", style=WIDE));
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 6 with a precomputed slider for the minimum wage
slider_figure(structure_of_models, "w_min", [0, 5, 10, 12, 15, 20], start=0, label="minimum wage")

Source. Adapted from Fig. 1.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • With the textbook’s inputs, the outcomes are \(w^* = 10\) and \(L^* = 50\), and nobody who wants to work at that wage is left out.
  • A minimum wage of 5 or 10 changes nothing, because it is not above the market wage. A minimum wage of 12 raises the wage to 12, cuts employment to 48, and leaves 6 hours of unemployment.
  • You never set the wage or employment directly: they are endogenous. You only change inputs, and the model works out the outcomes. That is what the textbook means by running an experiment with a model.

Your turn. Set the minimum wage to 15. How much unemployment does the model predict? Then check the number with labor_supply and labor_demand in the cell below.

Hint

Unemployment is labor_supply(15) - labor_demand(15), with the default values of a, l and f.

The long run and the short run

One chart organizes the whole textbook: the steady rise of U.S. income per person over 150 years, and the swings around that trend.

Fig. 7: Per capita GDP in the United States

Goal. See the three features of the graph that organizes the whole textbook: long-run growth, short-run fluctuations, and the question of what comes next.

The file has two columns. gdppc_actual is real GDP per person. gdppc_potential is potential output: what GDP per person would be if prices were fully flexible and all resources were fully employed. From 1949 on, potential output comes from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO); before 1949 it is a smooth statistical trend of the actual series, so the early years should be read with care.

usgdp = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig1-7.csv")
usgdp.head()
year gdppc_actual gdppc_potential
0 1870 4634 4583
1 1871 4746 4661
2 1872 4817 4740
3 1873 4937 4823
4 1874 4791 4911

The average annual growth rate \(g\) between 1870 and 2025 is the constant rate that turns the 1870 value into the 2025 value in 155 years: \(y_{2025} = y_{1870}(1+g)^{155}\) (equation 3), so \(g = (y_{2025}/y_{1870})^{1/155} - 1\) (equation 4).

Python note. usgdp.set_index("year").gdppc_actual gives a column whose rows are labeled by year, so y[2025] is the 2025 value.

y = usgdp.set_index("year").gdppc_actual
g = (y[2025] / y[1870]) ** (1 / 155) - 1
print(f"Average annual growth, 1870-2025: {100 * g:.2f}%")
Average annual growth, 1870-2025: 1.88%

The same chart can be drawn for any country in the Maddison file of Fig. 1. Only the United States has an official estimate of potential output (from the CBO), so other countries show actual GDP per person only.

Python note. data.iloc[0] is the first row and data.iloc[-1] the last, so the growth formula uses each country’s own first and last year. On a ratio-scale axis, an annotation’s height is also given in powers of ten: y=np.log10(30000).

def per_capita_chart(country="United States"):
    """Fig. 1.7: per capita GDP on a ratio scale with its average growth rate (U.S.: also potential)."""
    if country == "United States":
        data = usgdp.rename(columns={"gdppc_actual": "Actual", "gdppc_potential": "Potential"})
        series = ["Actual", "Potential"]
    else:
        data = world[world.country == country].rename(columns={"gdppc": "Actual"})
        series = ["Actual"]
    first, last = data.iloc[0], data.iloc[-1]
    growth = (last.Actual / first.Actual) ** (1 / (last.year - first.year)) - 1
    fig = px.line(data, x="year", y=series, log_y=True, color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
                  labels={"year": "Year", "value": "Per capita GDP (2022 dollars, ratio scale)", "variable": "Series"},
                  title=f"{country}: GDP per person grew {round(100 * growth, 1) + 0.0:.1f}% a year, "
                        f"{first.year:.0f}–{last.year:.0f}")       # + 0.0: no -0.0
    fig.update_traces(selector=dict(name="Potential"), line_dash="dash")
    low = 3500 if data.Actual.min() >= 3500 else (1000 if data.Actual.min() >= 1000 else 400)
    high = 100000 if data.Actual.max() <= 100000 else 250000
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[500, 1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000],
                     range=[np.log10(low), np.log10(high)])
    fig.update_xaxes(range=[1865, 2030])
    fig.add_annotation(x=1870, y=np.log10(0.8 * high), showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font=dict(size=14),
                       text=f"Income in {last.year:.0f}: {last.Actual / first.Actual:.1f} times<br>its {first.year:.0f} level")
    return fig
interact(per_capita_chart,
         country=Dropdown(options=sorted(world.country.unique()), value="United States", description="country"));
